name: Barbara Jones
chief_complaint: Difficulty breathing and facial swelling after eating at a restaurant
opening_statement: I'm having trouble breathing and my face is really swollen. I think I ate something with peanuts in it about 10 minutes ago.
emotional_baseline: Anxious and frightened, speaking in short sentences due to respiratory distress

symptoms.character: Tight chest with audible wheeze, sensation of throat closing
symptoms.timing: Immediate onset after eating Thai curry

rag_citations.content: Anaphylaxis presents with respiratory symptoms including bronchospasm, wheeze, stridor, and upper airway oedema within minutes of allergen exposure

symptoms.character: Rapid swelling of lips, tongue, and periorbital regions

rag_citations.content: Angioedema affecting face, lips, and tongue is a characteristic feature of anaphylaxis and indicates airway compromise risk

symptoms.character: Widespread raised, erythematous, pruritic welts across trunk and limbs

rag_citations.content: Cutaneous manifestations including urticaria and angioedema occur in 80-90% of anaphylaxis cases and often precede cardiovascular or respiratory symptoms
Cardiovascular manifestations including hypotension, tachycardia, and presyncope indicate severe anaphylaxis requiring immediate adrenaline

symptoms.character: Feeling sick in stomach, no vomiting yet

past_medical_history.details: Diagnosed after urticarial reaction to peanut butter. Previous mild reactions managed with antihistamines. Never required adrenaline before.
Well-controlled on preventer therapy. Uses salbutamol PRN approximately twice weekly. No hospital admissions. Last spirometry 12 months ago normal.
Managed with intranasal corticosteroid during spring. Grass pollen triggers.

medications.name: Salbutamol inhaler
medications.compliance: Uses approximately 2-3 times per week for exercise-induced symptoms

medications.name: Mometasone nasal spray
medications.dose: 2 sprays each nostril daily during spring

allergies: PEANUTS (confirmed IgE-mediated, previous urticaria, current anaphylaxis). Grass pollen (rhinitis). No drug allergies known.
family_history: Mother has asthma and eczema. Father has seasonal allergic rhinitis. Younger brother (age 22) has tree nut allergy. No family history of cardiovascular disease or autoimmune conditions.

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker - 4-6 standard drinks per week
social_history.exercise: Runs 3 times per week, attends yoga classes
social_history.diet: Generally healthy, strictly avoids peanuts and peanut-containing products
social_history.adrenaline_autoinjector: Was prescribed EpiPen 3 years ago but did not fill prescription as 'never needed it before'. Does not carry adrenaline autoinjector.

examination_findings.general: Anxious, distressed, sitting upright, able to speak in short sentences only
examination_findings.airway: Patent but at risk - visible tongue and lip swelling, reports sensation of throat tightness
examination_findings.respiratory: Bilateral expiratory wheeze throughout lung fields, using accessory muscles, prolonged expiratory phase
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, weak peripheral pulses, capillary refill 3 seconds, heart sounds normal
examination_findings.skin: Widespread urticarial rash across trunk, arms, and legs. Erythematous raised welts 0.5-3cm diameter. Marked angioedema of lips, periorbital regions, and tongue.
examination_findings.neurological: Alert but anxious, GCS 15, no focal neurology

immediate.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 118 bpm, no ischemic changes
immediate.peak_flow: Not performed due to severity of presentation

serum_tryptase.timing: Sample taken 90 minutes after symptom onset
serum_tryptase.interpretation: Peak tryptase >25 mcg/L diagnostic of anaphylaxis when taken 1-2 hours after event

after_stabilization.chest_xray: Clear lung fields, no consolidation or pneumothorax

follow_up.skin_prick_testing: To be performed by immunologist as outpatient - confirm peanut sensitivity and screen for other food allergens
follow_up.specific_ige: Arachis hypogaea (peanut) IgE to be checked if skin testing unavailable

expected_management.rationale: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. IM adrenaline into anterolateral thigh. May repeat after 5 minutes if inadequate response.
Hypoxia due to bronchospasm and airway oedema requires supplemental oxygen

expected_management.intervention: Establish IV access and commence 0.9% sodium chloride rapid infusion
expected_management.rationale: Fluid resuscitation for hypotension. Give 1-2L bolus rapidly if BP remains low.

expected_management.intervention: Position patient supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress worsens)
expected_management.rationale: Improves venous return and blood pressure in distributive shock
Adjunct bronchodilator for persistent wheeze. Does NOT replace adrenaline.
May prevent biphasic reaction (occurs in 20% of cases). Not acute treatment.
Antihistamine for urticaria and itch. Adjunct only, does NOT treat airway or cardiovascular features.

expected_management.intervention: Continuous monitoring: ECG, BP, SpO2, RR
expected_management.rationale: Monitor for response to treatment and detect biphasic reactions
Biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% of anaphylaxis cases, typically 4-8 hours after initial event
Essential for future self-management. Provide education on recognition and use. PBS authority required.
expected_management.pbs_restriction: Streamlined authority code 4453 - patients with previous anaphylaxis

expected_management.rationale: Confirm allergen via skin prick testing, consider component-resolved diagnostics, discuss cross-reactivity with tree nuts, provide action plan

expected_management.intervention: Provide ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis
expected_management.rationale: Written emergency management plan. Download from www.allergy.org.au
Asthma is a risk factor for severe anaphylaxis. Ensure optimal control and patient has current asthma action plan.
Alerts emergency responders to peanut allergy in future unconscious presentations

critical_errors.error: Failure to administer intramuscular adrenaline as first-line treatment
critical_errors.consequence: Anaphylaxis is life-threatening. Delayed adrenaline administration significantly increases mortality risk. Antihistamines and corticosteroids DO NOT treat airway obstruction or cardiovascular collapse.
critical_errors.correct_action: Administer IM adrenaline 0.5mg (0.5mL of 1:1000) into anterolateral thigh within 60 seconds of recognizing anaphylaxis

critical_errors.error: Administering adrenaline intravenously instead of intramuscularly in conscious patient
critical_errors.consequence: IV adrenaline in non-arrest situations causes cardiac arrhythmias, hypertensive crisis, myocardial infarction. Reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock under specialist guidance.
critical_errors.correct_action: IM adrenaline is the correct route for anaphylaxis. IV adrenaline only if cardiac arrest or under ICU/anaesthetic supervision with infusion pump.

critical_errors.error: Discharging patient without adrenaline autoinjector prescription and education
critical_errors.consequence: Patient at high risk of recurrent severe anaphylaxis. Without autoinjector, may not survive future exposure before ambulance arrives.
critical_errors.correct_action: Prescribe 2x EpiPen 300mcg (PBS authority code 4453), provide ASCIA action plan, demonstrate autoinjector technique, arrange follow-up with allergist

critical_errors.error: Failure to observe patient for minimum 4-6 hours after stabilization
critical_errors.consequence: Biphasic reactions occur in 20% of anaphylaxis cases, typically 4-8 hours later. Premature discharge risks unmonitored deterioration at home.
critical_errors.correct_action: Minimum 4-6 hour observation period, longer if risk factors present (severe initial reaction, previous biphasic reaction, ongoing symptoms)

critical_errors.error: Treating with antihistamines or corticosteroids alone without adrenaline
critical_errors.consequence: Antihistamines treat urticaria only. Corticosteroids prevent biphasic reactions but have no acute effect. Neither treats bronchospasm or hypotension. Patient may die from delayed adrenaline.
critical_errors.correct_action: Adrenaline is the ONLY first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only.

critical_errors.error: Administering adrenaline subcutaneously instead of intramuscularly
critical_errors.consequence: Subcutaneous absorption is slow and unpredictable, especially in hypotensive patients. Delays therapeutic effect in time-critical emergency.
critical_errors.correct_action: Always use IM route into anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis muscle) for rapid, reliable absorption

fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent Medium-difficulty case for AMC clinical exam. Scenario accurately reflects time-critical anaphylaxis presentation with clear diagnostic criteria (acute onset, multi-system involvement within minutes of allergen exposure). Critical errors appropriately focus on life-threatening omissions: delayed adrenaline, wrong route, inadequate observation. The comorbid asthma increases severity risk and is correctly identified as requiring review. Patient's lack of adrenaline autoinjector despite known allergy is realistic and highlights common compliance gap. eTG citations are accurate and specific to Australian guidelines. Management plan aligns with ASCIA recommendations including PBS authority requirements for EpiPen. Biphasic reaction risk appropriately emphasized. Difficulty calibration correct: 3 comorbidities (asthma, allergic rhinitis, known peanut allergy), time-critical presentation requiring immediate intervention = Medium difficulty. Would recommend for AMC candidates learning emergency allergy management.

Well-constructed anaphylaxis case with appropriate progression from cutaneous to respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms. Timeline (symptoms within 10 minutes of allergen exposure) meets diagnostic criteria. The inclusion of serum tryptase investigation demonstrates understanding of confirmatory testing (sample timing 1-2 hours post-event is correct). Social history detail regarding non-compliance with EpiPen prescription is clinically important and common in young adults with childhood-onset allergies. Critical errors correctly identify most dangerous mistakes: IV adrenaline in conscious patients (causes arrhythmias), subcutaneous route (slow absorption), and discharge without autoinjector (high recurrence risk). Learning objectives should emphasize ASCIA Action Plan and component-resolved diagnostics for cross-reactivity assessment. Minor suggestion: could add specific IgE levels to peanut components (Ara h 1, 2, 3) to enhance educational value for specialist trainees, but not essential for AMC clinical exam level. PBS restriction code 4453 for EpiPen is correct. MBS item 16500 for ED Category 3 attendance appropriate. Overall: clinically accurate, educationally valuable, difficulty well-calibrated. Approved for AMC examination purposes.

learning_objectives: Recognize anaphylaxis using clinical criteria: acute onset multi-system involvement (skin/mucosal + respiratory OR cardiovascular) within minutes-hours of allergen exposure
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 0.5mg (0.5mL of 1:1000) as first-line treatment for anaphylaxis - IM route into anterolateral thigh is critical for rapid absorption
Understand that antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only - they DO NOT treat airway obstruction or cardiovascular collapse in anaphylaxis
Recognize biphasic reactions occur in 20% of anaphylaxis cases, requiring minimum 4-6 hour observation period after stabilization
Prescribe adrenaline autoinjectors (2x EpiPen 300mcg) at discharge with PBS authority code 4453, provide ASCIA Action Plan, and demonstrate technique
Identify asthma as risk factor for severe anaphylaxis - review asthma control and ensure patient has current asthma action plan
Understand serum tryptase timing: sample taken 1-2 hours after symptom onset, level >25 mcg/L confirms mast cell activation in anaphylaxis
Refer to clinical immunologist for skin prick testing, specific IgE testing, and assessment of cross-reactivity with other allergens (tree nuts, legumes)
